prompt: You are reviewing an online migration of a synthetic multi-tenant event service. Produce a concrete safe design and migration/rollback sequence, not code edits. Identify the few issues that decide correctness, compare at least two workable paths, and propose the cheapest tests that could disprove your preferred path. State unknowns rather than inventing facts. Use only supplied materials. Final answer: at most 600 English words, with sections Decision, Evidence and assumptions, Alternatives, Failure modes, Falsification tests, and Open questions. Every new proposal should explain why it could work, what would falsify it, and the cheapest check. This is a closed-material analysis; do not browse or inspect unrelated files.

materials.title: Synthetic service specification and rollout proposal
materials.text:
SPEC-1: Authenticated HTTP ingress knows tenant_id. An upstream producer assigns event_id unique only within that tenant. Delivery is at least once. Normal retries can last 7 days; approved historical imports may replay an event after 45 days. Payloads carry a per-order sequence number. Cancel and reserve events are not commutative.
SPEC-2: HTTP handlers enqueue JSON containing event_id, order_id, operation and sequence. Workers use a pooled database connection. The proposed tenant context is connection-local session state. Worker crashes, connection reuse and concurrent handling are ordinary. There is no permanent producer-to-tenant mapping outside the queued payload.
SPEC-3: PostgreSQL currently stores legacy orders by numeric order_id. Two customer databases will merge into one tenant-keyed schema. Numeric order IDs overlap. New code plans orders_v2(tenant_id, order_id, status, last_sequence) and an idempotency ledger processed(event_id PRIMARY KEY, created_at). Old workers ignore tenant_id and still update orders_v1.
SPEC-4: Proposed worker flow: check processed; if absent update order state, commit; call an external billing API; insert processed and acknowledge. Billing accepts a caller-supplied idempotency key and retains it for 24 hours, but offers no transaction spanning our database and billing. An API timeout does not tell us whether charging occurred.
SPEC-5: Proposed rollout: backfill v1 to v2 while dual-writing sequentially to both tables, switch readers, then remove tenant-specific v1 routing and drop v1 after 24 hours. Operations requires rollback for 72 hours after switching. Some new events create records that do not exist in v1. A queue drain can pause one tenant for at most 60 seconds; global downtime is not allowed.
SPEC-6: Observability includes worker ID, event ID and timestamps but currently omits tenant and schema epoch. Dashboards report aggregate success and queue lag, not per-tenant reconciliation. Ledger pruning is proposed after 24 hours to bound size. Every design must explain what happens to unresolved external effects and old queued messages.

materials.title: Synthetic incident traces (facts, not a supplied diagnosis)
materials.text:
TRACE-A: Tenant amber event e17 is acknowledged. Tenant blue later sends its own e17 for an unrelated order; it is acknowledged without an order change.
TRACE-B: Worker w2 commits order reserve at 10:00:00.010, billing request times out at .300, and w2 exits before processed insert. At 10:00:04 a redelivery is handled by w3. Billing reconciliation later lists two attempted charge requests but does not resolve charge outcome.
TRACE-C: Backfill reads order 88 at status pending. A new event updates v1 then v2 to cancelled. Backfill subsequently writes its earlier pending snapshot into v2.
TRACE-D: Connection c7 last served amber; it is later returned to the pool, then used for blue. Query logs show order_id but do not record active tenant context. No cross-tenant leak has been proven by the supplied logs.
TRACE-E: At the switch, an older cancel message with sequence 11 arrives after reserve sequence 12. The old queue payload has no schema epoch. The rollback exercise restores old readers but ignores records first created in v2.
